newsitem.title: USA: Oil jumps on new Iraq tensions; sets post-Gulf high.
newsitem.headline: Oil jumps on new Iraq tensions; sets post-Gulf high.

text.p: Oil prices soared Wednesday, setting a post-Gulf war high in London after Iraq fired at U.S. fighter planes flying over the north of the country.
On the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil closed up 63 cents to $24.75 a barrel after jumping to $24.98 -- the highest since mid-April, when it hit a post-Gulf war peak of $25.70 a barrel.
In London, crude oil jumped to $23.82 a barrel -- the highest since $31.20 in the heat of Operation Desert Storm in January 1991 -- before retreating to $23.61, still 73 cents above Tuesday's close.
Unleaded gasoline gained 1.06 cents to close at 65.91 cents a gallon on the NYMEX and heating oil was up 1.52 cents to 68.19 cents a gallon.
"Clearly the Iraqi events overnight was the fundamental reason here, and that brought in a lot of funding buying" said Gerry Samuels, managing director of ARB Oil.
A senior U.S. defence official, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters that one or two surface-to-air missiles were fired at two U.S. F-16 fighter jets Wednesday.
The missiles missed their targets but the United States also moved B-52 bombers to a base in the Indian Ocean to back its threat of new military strikes on Iraq.

While further military action over Iraq poses little threat to the region's key oil supplies in Saudi Arabia, Iran and Kuwait, it should continue to deprive the market of 600,000 to 700,000 barrels a day of Iraqi oil that was expected to come from the since-halted U.N. food-for-oil agreement with Iraq.
"Nobody wants to be caught short on this thing. The onus is on the short side," said Al Lindeth, a trader with GSC Energy.

Prices jumped $1 a barrel last week after Iraqi troops moved into Iraqi Kurdistan in support of a Kurdish faction, drawing U.S. retaliatory attacks against targets in the south of Iraq and forcing the United Nations to cancel the agreement to allow Iraq to resume limited oil exports to allow it to buy food and medicines.

Iraq, whose exports have been under a U.N. embargo since it invaded Kuwait in August 1990, was to have been allowed to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to pay for food and medical supplies.
In anticipation of Iraqi oil sales, some refiners had allowed their reserves to run low and subsequently had to scramble to cover requirements at higher prices.
Industry data released Tuesday showed that U.S. oil stocks fell by more than 6.5 million barrels at Gulf Coast and East Coast refineries last week.
Heating oil stocks, of increasing importance as the winter approaches, rose by three million barrels but remain at just 70 percent of levels this time last year in the northeastern United States.
"Heating oil still remains the strongest in the (oil) complex. Its inventories are still really low," said Tom Bentz, an analyst with ING Derivatives.
